lessons.conclusion_html:
Conclusion

The invasion of Czechoslovakia killed appeasement and led to the guarantee to Poland. The Nazi-Soviet Pact removed Soviet opposition and gave Hitler the confidence to invade, making war almost certain.

Key Takeaways

  • Appeasement died in Prague: Hitler’s March 1939 invasion proved his aims went beyond self-determination. Britain and France finally committed to resisting him with the guarantee to Poland.
  • The Pact was a cynical bargain: Hitler avoided a two-front war and gained resources. Stalin gained time to rearm, territory, and a buffer zone. Both knew it was temporary.
  • Western failures pushed Stalin toward Hitler: Exclusion from Munich, the weak Drax mission, and distrust of the Poland guarantee convinced Stalin that signing with Germany was his best option — sealing Poland’s fate.

lessons.title: The Outbreak of War
lessons.description: Germany’s invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939, Britain’s ultimatum, and the declaration of World War Two.
lessons.content_html:
The Final Target: Poland

With the Nazi-Soviet Pact securing his eastern flank, Hitler turned on Poland. He demanded the return of Danzig (a “Free City” under the League of Nations with a majority German population) and the end of the Polish Corridor — the strip of land separating East Prussia from the rest of Germany.

Poland stood firm. Unlike Czechoslovakia, Poland had a clear guarantee from Britain and France. After Hitler broke his promise over Czechoslovakia, they had committed to defending Poland. Hitler gambled they would back down again. This time, he was wrong.

The Gleiwitz Incident

On 31 August 1939, German SS troops staged a Gleiwitz Incident — a false flag operation. Nazis dressed as Polish soldiers attacked several radio and communications centres on the German border near Gleiwitz. They left behind the body of a concentration camp prisoner in a Polish uniform to make it look real.

Key Fact

The Gleiwitz Incident was a manufactured pretext. Hitler needed an excuse to claim Germany was acting in “self-defence.” Every detail was planned by the SS under orders from Berlin. The invasion had been prepared weeks in advance.

The Invasion of Poland

On 1 September 1939, Germany invaded Poland using Blitzkrieg — “Lightning War.” This new form of warfare combined speed, technology, and overwhelming force. Yet again, Hitler claimed Germany was acting in self-defence.

Blitzkrieg used coordinated air and ground attacks. Panzers (tanks) smashed through Polish defences in armoured columns, while Stukas (dive-bombers) destroyed communications and supply lines from the air.

The Polish army, though brave, was overwhelmed. Much of it relied on horse-mounted cavalry and outdated equipment — no match for German armour and air power. The speed of advance meant Poland could not organise an effective defence.

On 17 September, the Soviet Red Army invaded Poland from the east — as agreed in the Nazi-Soviet Pact’s secret clause. Caught between two armies, Poland was hopeless. Warsaw surrendered on 27 September. Poland was divided between Germany and the USSR.

Britain and France Declare War

On 3 September 1939, Britain and France both gave ultimatums to Germany: leave Poland or face war. They had promised to do this after Hitler broke his word over Czechoslovakia.

Germany ignored the threat. At 11:15 am on 3 September 1939, Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain addressed the nation by radio:

Key Fact — Chamberlain’s Broadcast

“I am speaking to you from the Cabinet Room at 10 Downing Street. This morning the British Ambassador in Berlin handed the German Government a final note stating that, unless we heard from them by 11 o’clock that they were prepared at once to withdraw their troops from Poland, a state of war would exist between us. I have to tell you now that no such undertaking has been received, and that consequently this country is at war with Germany.”

France declared war later that day. The guarantee to Poland had been honoured. After a decade of tension, failed diplomacy, and appeasement, Europe was at war again. It took just four weeks to defeat Poland.

Timeline: The Outbreak of War

31 August 1939

The Gleiwitz Incident

SS troops dress as Polish soldiers and attack German border targets. Hitler uses this as a pretext to claim “self-defence.”

1 September 1939

Germany invades Poland

Blitzkrieg is unleashed. Panzers and Stukas devastate Polish defences.

3 September 1939

Britain and France declare war

Both give ultimatums: leave Poland or face war. Germany ignores them. At 11:15 am, Chamberlain announces Britain is at war. France follows that day.

17 September 1939

Soviet Union invades eastern Poland

The Red Army attacks from the east, as agreed in the Nazi-Soviet Pact. Poland is caught between two invaders.

27 September 1939

Warsaw surrenders

After four weeks, the Polish capital falls. Poland is divided between Germany and the USSR.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When assessing who caused the war, focus on individuals’ roles. Hitler was the most direct cause — he planned the invasion, manufactured the pretext, and gave the order. But also show how the Nazi-Soviet Pact made it possible by removing the two-front war threat. The best answers weigh both immediate and enabling causes.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Conclusion

The invasion of Poland was the direct cause of World War Two. Blitzkrieg crushed Poland in four weeks. Britain and France honoured their guarantee, ending a decade of tension and appeasement with a declaration of war.

Key Takeaways

  • Gleiwitz was a calculated lie: Hitler manufactured a pretext to justify invasion. The attack on Poland was premeditated — key evidence when assessing blame for the war.
  • Blitzkrieg changed warfare: Panzers, Stukas, and motorised infantry overwhelmed Poland in four weeks, shocking the world with Germany’s military power.
  • Britain and France finally acted: The guarantee to Poland was honoured — but years of appeasement had let Hitler grow far stronger than he might have been.

lessons.title: Responsibility for WWII
lessons.description: Weighing up the roles of Hitler, appeasement, the League’s failure and the Treaty of Versailles in causing war.
lessons.content_html:
Who Was to Blame?

World War Two was not caused by one person or one event. It grew from twenty years of tension — flawed treaties, failed institutions, and bad decisions on all sides. The best exam answers show war had multiple, connected causes.

Argument 1: Hitler Was Responsible

This is the most direct argument. Hitler’s aims, set out in Mein Kampf (1925), could not be achieved without war. He wanted to overturn the Treaty of Versailles, unite all German speakers, seize Lebensraum in the east, and destroy Communism. The Hossbach Memorandum (1937) confirmed these plans. In a secret meeting with his generals, Hitler said Germany could only get the raw materials it needed by expanding east. He named Austria, Czechoslovakia, Poland, and Lithuania as targets, and said this must happen as soon as possible. War with Britain was to be avoided — but war itself was inevitable.

Hitler broke every agreement he made. He rearmed Germany, remilitarised the Rhineland, carried out Anschluss with Austria, seized the Sudetenland, invaded Czechoslovakia, and finally invaded Poland. He also built alliances — the Rome–Berlin Axis (1936) with Italy, the Anti-Comintern Pact (1936) with Japan, and the Pact of Steel (1939) with Italy — making Germany stronger at each step.

Each move was calculated. He tested Britain and France and found them weak. The invasion of Poland was the direct cause of war — Hitler planned it, manufactured the Gleiwitz pretext, and gave the order.

Historians debate whether Hitler had a master plan from the start (the “intentionalist” view) or was an opportunist who seized chances as they came (the “structuralist” view). The Hossbach Memorandum supports the intentionalist view. Either way, his actions were the main driver of war.

Argument 2: Chamberlain & Appeasement

Hitler was the aggressor — but the policy of appeasement by Britain and France encouraged him. By giving in again and again, the Western powers told Hitler that aggression would be rewarded and that they lacked the will to fight.

The Munich Agreement (1938) is the clearest example. Britain and France let Hitler take the Sudetenland without a fight, betraying Czechoslovakia. This gave Hitler the confidence to seize the rest of Czechoslovakia just months later.

Appeasement gave Hitler time to rearm. Germany’s military grew far faster than Britain’s. Each concession made the eventual war harder to win. Appeasement also alienated Stalin — being excluded from Munich pushed him toward signing the Nazi-Soviet Pact with Hitler instead.

Context matters, though. Britain was still recovering from World War One. The public feared another war. The military was not ready to fight in 1938. Chamberlain may have been wrong, but his reasoning was not irrational.

Argument 3: Stalin Was Responsible

The Nazi-Soviet Pact (August 1939) sealed Poland’s fate. By signing with Hitler, Stalin removed the threat of a two-front war — the one thing that might have stopped the invasion of Poland.

The Pact’s secret clause agreed to divide Poland between Germany and the USSR. Stalin did not just stand aside — he invaded Poland from the east on 17 September 1939.

Stalin acted out of self-interest. He gained territory, time to rearm, and a buffer zone of Baltic states. He calculated that letting the Western nations fight Germany would help the USSR.

However, Stalin’s defenders say he was pushed toward the Pact by Western failures. He had been excluded from Munich and distrusted the guarantee to Poland. He believed Britain and France wanted to redirect Hitler eastward. Without the Nazi-Soviet Pact, Hitler may never have risked invading Poland — he would have faced a war on two fronts.

Argument 4: Wider Factors

Beyond individual leaders, deeper factors created the conditions that made war possible — even likely.

Key Fact — Long-Term Causes
  • The Treaty of Versailles (1919) — created deep German resentment. The “Diktat,” War Guilt Clause, reparations, territorial losses, and military limits all fuelled a desire for revenge that Hitler exploited.
  • The League of Nations — failed to stop aggression in Manchuria (1931) and Abyssinia (1935). This proved collective security was an empty promise. Dictators learned they could act without punishment.
  • The Great Depression (1929) — mass unemployment and poverty created the conditions for extremism. Without the Depression, Hitler would probably never have risen to power. Many countries acted in self-interest rather than working together, and some turned to aggressive dictators who promised easy answers.

The Treaty of Versailles was a long-term cause. It did not make war certain, but it created resentment that extremists exploited. Hitler’s promise to overturn the Treaty was central to his appeal.

The League of Nations was meant to prevent wars through collective action. It failed — unable to stop Japan in Manchuria or Italy in Abyssinia. This showed Hitler that no one would stand up to aggression.

The Great Depression (1929) turned German resentment into revolution. Millions lost jobs and hope, making them willing to vote for extreme parties. Without the Depression, the Nazis might have stayed a fringe movement. Aggressive leaders across Europe used their militaries to grab the resources they wanted.
lessons.exam_tip_html: This is a classic “who was to blame?” essay topic. The exam question will name one cause and ask “How far do you agree?” — e.g. appeasement, Hitler’s foreign policy, the Nazi-Soviet Pact, or German remilitarisation. Start with that given factor, then add two more causes to show balance. Always reach a clear judgement in your conclusion — explain why one cause matters more than the others. Strong answers weigh causes against each other, not just list them.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Conclusion

There was no single cause of World War Two. Hitler’s ambition drove Europe toward war, but he was helped by a flawed treaty, a weak League, appeasement that rewarded aggression, and a Soviet pact that removed the last barrier to invasion. The war was the result of collective failure over two decades.

Key Takeaways

  • Hitler bears the greatest responsibility: His aims could not be achieved without war. He broke every agreement, manufactured pretexts, and ordered the invasion of Poland.
  • He did not act alone: Appeasement emboldened him, the Nazi-Soviet Pact enabled him, and the failures of Versailles, the League, and the Depression brought him to power. These causes are connected — for example, appeasement alienated Stalin, pushing him toward the Pact with Hitler.
  • Think in layers: Short-term triggers (Poland invasion), medium-term policies (appeasement, the Pact), and long-term factors (Versailles, League failure, Depression) all interacted. Always weigh them against each other and reach a clear judgement.
